items.title: Japan's debt-to-GDP is over 250% — and it hasn't defaulted
items.claim: Japan's general government gross debt was around 263% of GDP in 2023 (IMF). What's the orthodox explanation for why this hasn't triggered a sovereign debt crisis?

options.text: Japan does not actually have debt

Debt is mostly held domestically (BOJ, pension funds, banks) in yen, with the BOJ controlling the curve; net debt is lower; current account surplus; large household savings. Foreign-currency emerging market debt is structurally different

items.reveal_title: Composition matters as much as level
items.reveal:
Reinhart and Rogoff's controversial 2010 'Growth in a Time of Debt' suggested debt above 90% of GDP harmed growth. Subsequent re-analysis (Herndon, Ash, Pollin 2013) found an Excel error and weaker results. The relationship between debt levels and outcomes depends heavily on currency denomination, holders, monetary regime and growth rates.

Greece (2010-12) and Sri Lanka (2022) had foreign-currency exposure that Japan lacks. The UK has a Liability Driven Investment (LDI) crisis in autumn 2022 despite much lower debt levels — composition and confidence matter.
items.why: Headline debt-to-GDP misleads about sustainability. Currency, holders, maturity profile, monetary regime and growth trajectory matter as much as the ratio itself.

items.title: US tariffs on China were largely absorbed by US importers
items.claim: Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2019) studied the incidence of 2018 US tariffs on Chinese imports. What did they find?

options.text: Chinese exporters paid the entire tariff
Nearly the full cost of the tariffs was passed through to US importers and consumers; producer prices in China barely changed. The 'tariffs hurt foreigners' framing did not match the price data

items.reveal:
Amiti, Redding and Weinstein analysed customs and price data through 2019. The pass-through was nearly complete to US importers; Chinese export prices for affected goods didn't drop substantially.

Fajgelbaum, Goldberg, Kennedy and Khandelwal (QJE 2020) confirmed the finding using different methods. Subsequent Biden-era tariffs (2024) followed similar patterns. The US-China tariffs reshaped supply chains (Vietnam, Mexico saw substantial increases in exports to the US) more than they raised significant revenue.
items.why: The political rhetoric of tariffs often diverges from the economic incidence. Trade policy effects are empirically measurable; the empirics often don't support the political framing.

items.title: Framing changes choices on identical outcomes
items.claim: Kahneman and Tversky's classic 'Asian disease' problem: identical mortality outcomes framed differently (lives saved vs lives lost) produce systematically different preferences. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Preferences are reference-dependent and influenced by framing: gains and losses are evaluated relative to a reference point, with losses weighted more heavily (loss aversion)

items.reveal:
Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 Science paper presented the Asian disease problem. The same outcomes framed positively (lives saved) vs negatively (lives lost) reversed majority preferences between sure and probabilistic options.

The finding contradicts expected utility theory's invariance axiom. Replications include consumer choice, medical decisions and policy framing. Nudge policy uses this finding by setting defaults (organ donation opt-out vs opt-in) and framing communications.
items.why: If preferences depend on framing, then the framer is a significant agent in any choice architecture. Standard economics' assumed invariance underestimates this.
